claim: The human kinome contains more than 500 eukaryotic protein kinases (EPKs).
source: The human kinome contains more than 500 eukaryotic protein kinases (EPKs), which regulate a diverse array of cellular processes (Manning et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Manning et al., 2002, which is a reference to established scientific literature.

claim: Eukaryotic protein kinases regulate a diverse array of cellular processes.
source: The human kinome contains more than 500 eukaryotic protein kinases (EPKs), which regulate a diverse array of cellular processes (Manning et al., 2002).

claim: The collection of human kinases has been expanded by the discovery of novel kinases that function specifically in the secretory pathway.
source: Recently, the collection of human kinases has been further expanded by the discovery of novel kinases that function specifically in the secretory pathway (Dudkiewicz et al., 2013; Sreelatha et al., 2015; Tagliabracci et al., 2013a, 2013b).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to Dudkiewicz et al., 2013; Sreelatha et al., 2015; Tagliabracci et al., 2013a, 2013b.

claim: Novel secretory pathway kinases are so divergent from canonical EPKs that they eluded earlier identification and were not included on the kinome tree.
source: These proteins are so divergent from the canonical EPKs that they eluded earlier identification and were not included on the kinome tree.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the context of the discovery of novel kinases and their divergence from canonical EPKs.

claim: Four-jointed is a Golgi kinase that phosphorylates atypical cadherins Fat and Dachsous to regulate planar cell polarity in Drosophila.
source: Among them, four-jointed, a Golgi kinase, phosphorylates atypical cadherins Fat and Dachsous to regulate planar cell polarity in Drosophila (Ishikawa et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ishikawa et al., 2008.

claim: Fam20C is the long-sought physiological casein kinase that phosphorylates many secreted proteins.
source: Fam20C is the long-sought physiological casein kinase that phosphorylates many secreted proteins (Tagliabracci et al., 2012, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Tagliabracci et al., 2012, 2015.

claim: Fam20B is a xylose kinase that regulates the biosynthesis of proteoglycans.
source: Fam20B is a xylose kinase that regulates the biosynthesis of proteoglycans (Koike et al., 2009; Wen et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Koike et al., 2009; Wen et al., 2014.

claim: Fam20A lacks intrinsic kinase activity and functions as a positive regulator of Fam20C.
source: Fam20A lacks intrinsic kinase activity and functions as a positive regulator of Fam20C (Cui et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cui et al., 2015.

claim: The crystal structure of Caenorhabditis elegans Fam20C orthologue reveals an atypical kinase architecture remotely related to the EPKs.
source: The crystal structure of Caenorhabditis elegans Fam20C orthologue reveals an atypical kinase architecture remotely related to the EPKs (Xiao et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Xiao et al., 2013.

claim: Mutations in the Fam20 proteins cause several diseases in humans including biomineralization defects.
source: Importantly, mutations in the Fam20 proteins cause several diseases in humans including biomineralization defects, underscoring the physiological significance of phosphorylation-regulated processes in the secretory pathway (Sreelatha et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sreelatha et al., 2015.

claim: Two members of the human kinome positioned near the root of the kinome tree have been found to function in the secretory pathway.
source: Interestingly, two members of the human kinome that were positioned near the root of the kinome tree, have been found to function in the secretory pathway.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the context of the discovery of VLK and POMK.

claim: Vertebrate lonesome kinase (VLK/PKDCC/SgK493) phosphorylates a wide range of extracellular and endoplasmic reticulum (ER) resident proteins on tyrosine residues.
source: Vertebrate lonesome kinase (VLK/PKDCC/SgK493) phosphorylates a wide range of extracellular and endoplasmic reticulum (ER) resident proteins on tyrosine residues (Bordoli et al., 2014; Kinoshita et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bordoli et al., 2014; Kinoshita et al., 2009.

claim: Protein O-mannose kinase (POMK, previously referred to as SgK196) is a carbohydrate kinase like Fam20B.
source: On the other hand, protein O-mannose kinase (POMK, previously referred to as SgK196) is a carbohydrate kinase like Fam20B, and plays a critical role for the biosynthesis of functional α-dystroglycan (α-DG) (Yoshida-Moriguchi et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yoshida-Moriguchi et al., 2013.

claim: POMK plays a critical role for the biosynthesis of functional α-dystroglycan (α-DG).
source: On the other hand, protein O-mannose kinase (POMK, previously referred to as SgK196) is a carbohydrate kinase like Fam20B, and plays a critical role for the biosynthesis of functional α-dystroglycan (α-DG) (Yoshida-Moriguchi et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yoshida-Moriguchi et al., 2013.

claim: α-DG is a subunit of the dystroglycan complex.
source: α-DG is a subunit of the dystroglycan complex, and binds to basement membrane molecules such as laminin to connect the extracellular matrix with the actin cytoskeleton (Barresi and Campbell, 2006; Yoshida-Moriguchi and Campbell, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Barresi and Campbell, 2006; Yoshida-Moriguchi and Campbell, 2015.

claim: α-DG binds to basement membrane molecules such as laminin to connect the extracellular matrix with the actin cytoskeleton.
source: α-DG is a subunit of the dystroglycan complex, and binds to basement membrane molecules such as laminin to connect the extracellular matrix with the actin cytoskeleton (Barresi and Campbell, 2006; Yoshida-Moriguchi and Campbell, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Barresi and Campbell, 2006; Yoshida-Moriguchi and Campbell, 2015.

claim: α-DG is a receptor for human pathogens including members of Old World arenaviruses such as the Lassa fever virus.
source: α-DG is also a receptor for human pathogens including members of Old World arenaviruses such as the Lassa fever virus (Cao et al., 1998; Jae et al., 2013).

claim: All functions of α-DG critically depend on proper glycosylation of α-DG.
source: All these functions critically depend on proper glycosylation of α-DG, an elaborate process that involves at least 17 different enzymes (Yoshida-Moriguchi and Campbell, 2015).

claim: Proper glycosylation of α-DG is an elaborate process that involves at least 17 different enzymes.
source: All these functions critically depend on proper glycosylation of α-DG, an elaborate process that involves at least 17 different enzymes (Yoshida-Moriguchi and Campbell, 2015).

claim: The modification of α-DG starts with a unique trisaccharide molecule GalNAc-β3-GlcNAc-β4-Man attached to Ser/Thr residues on α-DG.
source: The modification starts with a unique trisaccharide molecule GalNAc-β3-GlcNAc-β4-Man attached to Ser/Thr residues on α-DG (Yoshida-Moriguchi et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yoshida-Moriguchi et al., 2013.

claim: The mannose in the GalNAc-β3-GlcNAc-β4-Man trisaccharide is phosphorylated by POMK at the C6 hydroxyl position.
source: The mannose is then phosphorylated by POMK at the C6 hydroxyl position, to allow further glycan elongation by enzymes including Fukutin, FKRP, TMEM5, B4GAT1, and LARGE (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) (Gerin et al., 2016; Inamori et al., 2012; Jae et al., 2013; Kanagawa et al., 2016; Praissman et al., 2016; Willer et al., 2014; Yoshida-Moriguchi et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to Gerin et al., 2016; Inamori et al., 2012; Jae et al., 2013; Kanagawa et al., 2016; Praissman et al., 2016; Willer et al., 2014; Yoshida-Moriguchi et al., 2010.

claim: Phosphorylation of mannose by POMK allows further glycan elongation by enzymes including Fukutin, FKRP, TMEM5, B4GAT1, and LARGE.
source: The mannose is then phosphorylated by POMK at the C6 hydroxyl position, to allow further glycan elongation by enzymes including Fukutin, FKRP, TMEM5, B4GAT1, and LARGE (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) (Gerin et al., 2016; Inamori et al., 2012; Jae et al., 2013; Kanagawa et al., 2016; Praissman et al., 2016; Willer et al., 2014; Yoshida-Moriguchi et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to Gerin et al., 2016; Inamori et al., 2012; Jae et al., 2013; Kanagawa et al., 2016; Praissman et al., 2016; Willer et al., 2014; Yoshida-Moriguchi et al., 2010.

claim: POMK mutations cause a spectrum of congenital and limb-girdle muscular dystrophies.
source: POMK mutations cause a spectrum of congenital and limb-girdle muscular dystrophies, including the most severe presentation known as the Walker-Warburg syndrome, which is associated with brain and eye abnormalities and death in early childhood (Di Costanzo et al., 2014; Jae et al., 2013; von Renesse et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Di Costanzo et al., 2014; Jae et al., 2013; von Renesse et al., 2014.

claim: Walker-Warburg syndrome is the most severe presentation of POMK mutations and is associated with brain and eye abnormalities and death in early childhood.
source: POMK mutations cause a spectrum of congenital and limb-girdle muscular dystrophies, including the most severe presentation known as the Walker-Warburg syndrome, which is associated with brain and eye abnormalities and death in early childhood (Di Costanzo et al., 2014; Jae et al., 2013; von Renesse et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Di Costanzo et al., 2014; Jae et al., 2013; von Renesse et al., 2014.

claim: POMK was long considered a pseudokinase.
source: Despite compelling biochemical evidence in support of the kinase activity of POMK, its catalytic mechanism was puzzling, since it was long considered a pseudokinase.
evidence: This claim is based on the historical classification of POMK as a pseudokinase.

claim: Canonical EPKs feature several highly conserved structural elements that are essential for catalysis.
source: The canonical EPKs feature several highly conserved structural elements that are essential for catalysis, which are exemplified by the cAMP-dependent protein kinase (PKA), including Lys72PKA from strand β3 that coordinates ATP, Glu91PKA from helix αC that pairs with Lys72PKA, Asp166PKA in the H/YRD motif that serves as the catalytic base, and Asp184PKA in the DFG motif that functions as the primary metal-binding residue (Hanks and Hunter, 1995; Jura et al., 2011; Taylor and Kornev, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hanks and Hunter, 1995; Jura et al., 2011; Taylor and Kornev, 2011.

claim: None of the important catalytic residues or motifs found in canonical EPKs were found in POMK.
source: None of these important residues or motifs were found in POMK (Eyers and Murphy, 2013; Manning et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Eyers and Murphy, 2013; Manning et al., 2002.

claim: The crystal structure of Danio rerio POMK was determined in complex with Mg2+ ions, ADP, aluminum fluoride, and the GalNAc-β3-GlcNAc-β4-Man trisaccharide substrate.
source: Here we present the crystal structure of Danio rerio POMK in complex with Mg2+ ions, ADP, aluminum fluoride, and the GalNAc-β3-GlcNAc-β4-Man trisaccharide substrate, thereby providing a snapshot of the catalytic transition state of this unusual kinase.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript, including crystallization and structure determination.

claim: The crystal structure of Danio rerio POMK provides a snapshot of the catalytic transition state of this unusual kinase.
source: Here we present the crystal structure of Danio rerio POMK in complex with Mg2+ ions, ADP, aluminum fluoride, and the GalNAc-β3-GlcNAc-β4-Man trisaccharide substrate, thereby providing a snapshot of the catalytic transition state of this unusual kinase.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the structural data showing the complex with aluminum fluoride, which mimics the transition state.

claim: The active site of POMK is established by residues located in non-canonical positions.
source: The active site of POMK is established by residues located in non-canonical positions and is stabilized by a disulfide bridge.
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The active site of POMK is stabilized by a disulfide bridge.
source: The active site of POMK is established by residues located in non-canonical positions and is stabilized by a disulfide bridge.

claim: The GalNAc-β3-GlcNAc moiety mediates the majority of interactions with POMK.

claim: Expression of various POMK mutants in POMK knockout cells validated the functional requirements of critical residues.
source: Expression of various POMK mutants in POMK knockout cells further validated the functional requirements of critical residues.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript, including cell-based assays.

source: Homo sapiens POMK (HsPOMK) contains a type II transmembrane (TM) domain and a lumenal kinase domain (Figure 1A).

source: There are four potential N-linked glycosylation sites in its kinase domain, Asn67, Asn165, Asn220, and Asn235.

claim: POMK is highly conserved throughout evolution.
source: POMK is highly conserved throughout evolution (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).

claim: No glycosylation site is present in DrPOMK.

claim: DrPOMK is 58% identical to HsPOMK in the kinase domain.
source: Interestingly, no glycosylation site is present in DrPOMK, which is otherwise 58% identical to HsPOMK in the kinase domain and can efficiently phosphorylate the GalNAc-β3-GlcNAc-β4-Man trisaccharide (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).

claim: DrPOMK can efficiently phosphorylate the GalNAc-β3-GlcNAc-β4-Man trisaccharide.

source: To determine the binding affinity of POMK for the trisaccharide substrate GalNAc-β3-GlcNAc-β4-Man, we synthesized GalNAc-β3-GlcNAc-β4-Man attached to a 4-methylumbelliferyl group (GalNAc-β3-GlcNAc-β4-Man-α-MU or GGM-MU, Figure 5A) using chemical and enzymatic methods.

claim: The dissociation constant of GGM-MU binding to POMK is 30.2 μM.

claim: The MU group contribution to the glycan binding affinity is likely small or negligible.
source: We observed that the peak intensity of MU H3 proton decreased only slightly even when the Man H1 peak is nearly saturated (fully bound) by adding 64.2 μM POMK, indicating that the MU group is mobile and does not interact with the protein strongly (Figure 5—figure supplement 1). Therefore, the MU group contribution to the glycan binding affinity is likely small or negligible.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the NMR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.
